notes.text: Mourn — And pray for his restitution, which the following words imply he did. Oil - Which was used in the inauguration of kings. But here it is used in the designation of a king; for David was not actually made king by it, but still remained a subject. And the reason of this anticipation was the comfort of Samuel, and other good men, against their fears in case of Saul's death, and the assurance of David's title, which otherwise would have been doubtful. I have provided - This phrase is very emphatical, and implies the difference between this and the former king. Saul was a king of the people's providing, he was the product of their sinful desires: but this is a king of my own providing, to fulfil all my will, and to serve my glory.

Trembled — Because it was strange and unexpected to them, this being but an obscure town, and remote from Samuel, and therefore they justly thought there was some extraordinary reason for it. Peaceable - The Hebrew phrase, comest thou in peace, is as much as to say (in our phrase) is all well?

He sanctified — It seems evident that there was something peculiar in Jesse's invitation. For first, both he and his sons were invited, whereas the others were only invited for their own persons. Secondly, the different phrase here used, that he sanctified these, when he only bade the other sanctify themselves; argues a singular care of Samuel in their sanctification. Which makes it probable, that the rest were only to join with them in the act of sacrificing; but these, and only these, were invited to feast upon the remainders of the sacrifices.

Before him — That is, in this place where God is now present. For it is observable, that not only the sacrifice is said to be offered, but even the feast upon the remainders of it is said, to be eaten before the Lord, Deut. xii, 7, that is, before or near his altar, where God was present in a special manner. This I take to be the person I am sent to anoint: wherein yet be was mistaken, as other prophets sometimes were, when they hastily spake their own thoughts, before they had consulted God.
Seven — There are but seven named, 1 Chron. ii, 13-15, because one of them was either born of a concubine: or, died immediately after this time.

Keepeth sheep — And consequently is the most unfit of all my sons for that high employment. Either therefore he did not understand David's wisdom and valour, or he judged him unfit, by reason of his mean education. And God so ordered it by his providence, that David's choice might plainly appear to be God's work, and not Samuel's, or Jesse's. David signifies beloved: a fit name for so eminent a type of the Beloved Son. It is supposed, David was now about twenty years old. If so, his troubles by Saul lasted near ten years: for he was thirty years old when Saul died. Samuel having done this went to Ramah. He retired to die in peace, since his eyes had seen the salvation, even the scepter brought into the tribe of Judah.

Anointed him — David's brethren saw David's unction, yet did not understand, that he was anointed to the kingdom; but were only told by Samuel, that he was anointed to some great service, which hereafter they should know. Thus Jesse only, and David, understood the whole business, and his brethren were able to attest to that act of Samuel's anointing him, which, with other collateral evidences, was abundantly sufficient to prove David's right to the kingdom, if need should be. The spirit,&c., - That is, he was immediately endowed with extraordinary gifts of God's Spirit, as strength, and courage, and wisdom, and other excellent qualities which fitted him for, and put him upon noble attempts.

glossa.text: *Look not.* The elder sons of Isai being rejected, the least is chosen to the kingdom, because, the Jewish priesthood and the kingdom of the former people being despised, Christ was made the head of the lesser people, king and priest.

*The little one.* From the office of the flocks David was made king of men: but Christ was carried over from the sheepfold of the Jewish people to the kingdom of the nations. ((GREG., lib. I Moral., cap. 6; lib. XVIII, cap. 6.)) The devil, although he ever seeks the affliction of the just, etc., *as far as* there is no power but from God.

notes.text: Lie down — To repose myself at noon, as the manner was in those hot countries. Green - Where there is both delight and plenty of provisions.
Restoreth — Hebrew. He bringeth it back; from its errors and wandering. For - Not for any worth in me, but for the glory of his justice, and faithfulness, and goodness.
Thy rod and thy staff — Two words denoting the same thing, and both designing God's pastoral care over him.

A table — Thou furnishest me with plenty of provisions and comforts. Oil - With aromatic ointments, which were then used at great feasts; thy comforts delight my soul. Runneth over - Thou hast given me a plentiful portions, signified by the cup, given to the guests by the master of the feast. This psalm is generally thought to have been composed by David, upon bringing the ark of God from the house of Obed- edom, into the tabernacle which David had built for it, 2 Sam. vi, 12, 17. Wherein he hath a farther prospect to the temple, which he earnestly desired and intended to build. Moreover because the tabernacle, and temple, and ark, were types of Christ, and of his church and of heaven. David extended his thoughts to them also, or at least the Holy Ghost designed to comprehend them under these typical expressions. He shews God's sovereignty over the world, ver. 1, 2. Who shall receive his blessing, ver. 3-6. An exhortation to receive Christ, ver. 7-10. A psalm of David.

glossa.text: *A psalm of David.* ((CASS.)) The Prophet foretold the return of the people from Babylon. *The Lord ruleth me.* A psalm of mercy, enumerating ten graces, that all may hope in the mercy of God. ((AUG.)) The Church speaks of Christ.

*In a place of pasture.* ((CASS.)) The first grace, a place of pasture, that is, the divine word, which fattens those who meditate upon it. *Upon the water.* The second grace, the water of refreshment.

*My soul.* ((ID.)) The third grace, etc., *as far as* but first he brought me up upon the water of refreshment, first he converted my soul. *He hath led.* ((ID.)) The fourth, in that he led me upon the precepts of charity. *Upon the paths.* ((AUG.)) The narrower commandments and the more perfect counsels; as it were upon paths few just men walk, even as paths are narrower than roads.

*For though I shall walk.* ((CASS.)) The fifth, that in the shadow of death he fears no evils. *Thou art with me.* ((AUG.)) In the heart by faith, that after the shadow of death I may be with thee. *Thy rod.* ((CASS.)) The sixth, correction; or the rod is strictness, which converts vices. The staff is governance, which upholds the faithful.

*Thou hast prepared in my sight.* ((CASS.)) The seventh, the table of the Lord, the blessed banqueting, the fullness of faith, the heavenly food, of which the Apostle: *He that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh judgment to himself. In my sight a table:* even if not that of the wicked. Of this it is said: *But these at the table of the rich man,* that is, of Christ, *know that thou too must prepare the like,* that is, to suffer as he did. *Thou hast anointed:* the eighth, the anointing of the head, namely of Christ, which was dried up by no barrenness of sin, whence the rest of the members rejoice, because from the head the ointment ran down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, and unto the skirt of his garment. *And my chalice.* The ninth, the chalice, the blood of Christ, which so inebriates that it makes men sober. *Mine,* because I receive it. Or, thine, because thou givest it. The table and the chalice, flesh and blood, although they are one sacrament, yet under diverse species, because both are taken, are here set down separately.
*And mercy.* ((CASS.)) The tenth, mercy following after unto keeping, which goes before unto the conferring of grace.
*And that I may dwell.* ((HIER.)) This is joined to all the things above. As though: thou hast placed, thou hast brought up, thou hast led, etc., and this to the end that I may dwell.

notes.text: Ye were once darkness — Total blindness and ignorance. Walk as children of light - Suitably to your present knowledge.

The fruit of the light — Opposite to " the unfruitful works of darkness," chap. iv, 11. Is in - That is, consists in. Goodness and righteousness and truth - Opposite to the sins spoken of, chap. iv, 25,&c.
Reprove them — To avoid them is not enough.
In secret — As flying the light.

But all things which are reproved, are thereby dragged out into the light, and made manifest — Shown in their proper colours, by the light. For whatsoever doth make manifest is light - That is, for nothing but light, yea, light from heaven, can make anything manifest.

Wherefore he — God. Saith - In the general tenor of his word, to all who are still in darkness. Awake thou that steepest - In ignorance of God and thyself; in stupid insensibility. And arise from the dead - From the death of sin. And Christ shall give thee light - Knowledge, holiness, happiness.

glossa.text: *For the fruit,* etc. Now works of this kind are the fruit and the work of light. *And justice,* etc. Justice and truth are parts of goodness. And the sense is: *In all goodness and justice and truth.* That is, do you speak fittingly things just and true.

*Reprove.* With a gentle mind, as the Apostle says elsewhere. Do this, namely, that outwardly the rebuke may terribly resound, and inwardly the love of gentleness may be held. He joins two things, namely, that they communicate not by consenting, and that they reprove. For in these two ways the evil man does not stain thee, if thou consentest not, and if thou reprovest. And the Apostle embraced both, saying: *Do not communicate,* etc., that is, do not consent, praise and approve. And because it is little not to consent, he adds: *But rather reprove,* that is, rebuke, correct, restrain. And the sense is: Be not consenting to evils by approving them, nor negligent in reproving, nor proud in reproving insultingly.

*But all things.* As if: although it be shameful to tell the things which they themselves do, yet they must be reproved, because thus they are often made manifest through confession and penance: and therefore reproof must be made, because what is thus made manifest is turned into light; or those evil men are made manifest to themselves that they are evil, and therefore are to be reproved, because thus they begin to be light. *For every thing which are made manifest.* That is, the evil man, when he becomes known to himself to be evil, becomes light. *Is light.* That is, through penance he begins to be turned into good.
*Arise.* Through confession. *And rise up.* Through satisfaction.

notes.text: Who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind? — That is, was it for his own sins, or the sins of his parents? They suppose (as many of the Jews did, though without any ground from Scripture) that he might have sinned in a pre-existent state, before he came into the world.

Jesus answered, Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents — It was not the manner of our Lord to answer any questions that were of no use, but to gratify an idle curiosity. Therefore he determines nothing concerning this. The scope of his answer is, It was neither for any sins of his own, nor yet of his parents; but that the power of God might be displayed.

The night is coming — Christ is the light. When the light is withdrawn night comes, when no man can work - No man can do any thing toward working out his salvation after this life is ended. Yet Christ can work always. But he was not to work upon earth, only during the day, or season which was appointed for him.
I am the light of the world — I teach men inwardly by my Spirit, and outwardly by my preaching, what is the will of God; and I show them, by my example, how they must do it.

He anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay — This might almost have blinded a man that had sight. But what could it do toward curing the blind? It reminds us that God is no farther from the event, when he works either with, or without means, and that all the creatures are only that which his almighty operation makes them.

Go, wash at the pool of Siloam — Perhaps our Lord intended to make the miracle more taken notice of. For a crowd of people would naturally gather round him to observe the event of so strange a prescription, and it is exceeding probable, the guide who must have led him in traversing a great part of the city, would mention the errand he was going upon, and so call all those who saw him to a greater attention. From the fountain of Siloam, which was without the walls of Jerusalem, a little stream flowed into the city, and was received in a kind of basin, near the temple, and called the pool of Siloam. Which is, by interpretation, Sent - And so was a type of the Messiah, who was sent of God. He went and washed, and came seeing - He believed, and obeyed, and found a blessing. Had he been wise in his own eyes, and reasoned, like Naaman, on the impropriety of the means, he had justly been left in darkness. Lord, may our proud hearts be subdued to the methods of thy recovering grace! May we leave thee to choose how thou wilt bestow favours, which it is our highest interest to receive on any terms.
A man called Jesus — He seems to have been before totally ignorant of him.
Anointing the eyes — With any kind of medicine on the Sabbath, was particularly forbidden by the tradition of the elders.
This man is not of God — Not sent of God. How can a man that is a sinner - That is, one living in wilful sin, do such miracles?
What sayest thou of him, for that he hath opened thine eyes? — What inference dost thou draw herefrom?
He should be put out of the synagogue — That is be excommunicated.
Are ye also — As well as I, at length convinced and willing to be his disciples?
We know not whence he is — By what power and authority he does these things.

The man answered — Utterly illiterate as he was. And with what strength and clearness of reason! So had God opened the eyes of his understanding, as well as his bodily eyes. Why, herein is a marvelous thing, that ye - The teachers and guides of the people, should not know, that a man who has wrought a miracle, the like of which was never heard of before, must be from heaven, sent by God.

We — Even we of the populace, know that God heareth not sinners - Not impenitent sinners, so as to answer their prayers in this manner. The honest courage of this man in adhering to the truth, though he knew the consequence, ver. 22, gives him claim to the title of a confessor.
He could do nothing — Of this kind; nothing miraculous.
Born in sin — And therefore, they supposed, born blind. They cast him out - Of the synagogue; excommunicated him.
Having found him — For he had sought him.
Who is he, that I may believe? — This implies some degree of faith already. He was ready to receive whatever Jesus said.
Lord, I believe — What an excellent spirit was this man of! Of so deep and strong an understanding; (as he had just shown to the confusion of the Pharisees,) and yet of so teachable a temper!

For judgment am I come into the world — That is, the consequence of my coming will be, that by the just judgment of God, while the blind in body and soul receive their sight, they who boast they see, will be given up to still greater blindness than before.

If ye had been blind — Invincibly ignorant; if ye had not had so many means of knowing: ye would have had no sin - Comparatively to what ye have now. But now ye say - Ye yourselves acknowledge, Ye see, therefore your sin remaineth - Without excuse, without remedy.

glossa.text: *And passing by.* Not standing in the way of sinners, but beside the way of our mortality. *A blind man.* The blind man signifies the human race, in which blindness is natural, because, when the first man sinned, the fault grew ingrained by reason of nature; whence according to the mind every man is born blind.

*Neither hath this man sinned.* They did indeed sin, but it was not brought about by that sin that he should be born blind; rather this is the cause, *that the works of God should be made manifest in him.* That, by enlightening him and by signifying through him what he is to do in the blindness of the human race, the Son of God may be made manifest; whence he adds: *I must work.*

*As long as I am in the world.* Not only then was Christ the light in the world, but he is also always with the elect through faith unto the consummation of the age, and it is the time for working. That night is the infernal night, in which it is permitted to none to work, as neither was it permitted to the burning rich man; but there is only a time of receiving.

*And he made clay.* As he formed the first man out of the slime of the earth, so through the same kind of clay he re-formed the human race. Of spittle he made clay, because the Word was made flesh. The spittle is the wisdom which came forth from the mouth of the Most High. The earth is the flesh of Christ. *He anointed the eyes.* That is, he made him a catechumen, who believes the Word made flesh. The anointed man does not yet see, but is sent to wash, that is, to be baptized in the Sent One, that is, in Christ, on account of which the name of the pool is so interpreted. Baptized, baptized from his sins, he received the light.

*And he came seeing,* etc. It is asked: how did he heal this man without faith, when it is read that he healed no one outwardly without an inward healing? But this is said of those who were sick on account of their sins: this man was languishing not on account of sin, but for the glory of God.
*This man is not of God,* etc. He keeps the sabbath spiritually who is without sin; not they, who are servants of sin.

*What sayest thou,* etc. They seek a pretext for accusation, that he might be driven out of the synagogue, but be found by Christ. *But he said,* etc. Still anointed in heart: he confesses, yet he does not lie.

*Until they called,* etc. Mystically: the parents, that is the devil or the vices, who say. He is of age, let him speak for himself: they who are unwilling that a man confess Christ.

*Give glory to God: We know,* etc. To give glory to God is to speak the truth about someone as though God were present, that is: to confess that this man is not God, as we do, but a sinner.
*Why again,* etc. ((AUG.)) He is vexed at their hardness, having from a blind man been made one that sees, and now not bearing with the blind.
*They reviled him therefore.* According to their heart it is a curse. But what is said is to be desired by all, that they should be disciples of Christ.

*But this man we know not.* Above they had said: *This man we know:* whence here they say that they know not; but we say that we know not the things which we cast away. He is not known, he lies hid by humility, he is betrayed by the power of his signs: it is not known whence he is, and as God he enlightens the blind.
*Unless this man were of God,* etc. Their anger despised, he freely confesses the truth. For these things would not be done save by the Lord, nor by the disciples, unless God were in them.

*He was born wholly in sins.* That is, with closed eyes, which they say to be for the sins of the parents; but Christ heals the whole: outside, the eyes; within, he opens the heart. *And dost thou teach us? And they cast him out.* By questioning him so often that they might learn, they had made him a master; but ungrateful, they cast out the one who taught. Yet because he was expelled, he was the more made a Christian.
*Who is he,* etc. Still anointed, by these words he shows that he had long had a heart ready to believe, but had not known in whom he ought to believe.
*And thou hast seen.* Now the Lord washes the face of the anointed, now he enlightens the eyes of the heart, and he confesses not only the Son of man but also the Son of God.

*That they who see not.* That is, they who think that they see seek to see; and they who see, that is, they who think that they see and do not seek the physician; and this is the judgment, that is, the discernment which distinguishes the cause of believers from the proud. For he will execute the judgment of damnation not now, but at the end; whence: *I judge not any man.*

The King of love my shepherd is
O Thou, in whose presence my soul takes delight

praise.title: Light of the World (Here I Am to Worship)

echoes.text: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.
echoes.note: 'You were once darkness, but are now light' draws on 'the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light,' the prophetic light/darkness reversal. High coherence with Ephesians' conversion-as-illumination motif and strong verbal volume in the light/walk pairing.

echoes.text: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you.
echoes.note: 'Arise, shine, for your light has come' anchors both the light-children theme here and explicitly the hymn of v.14. The Septuagintal phoatizou/anastethi cluster is verbally present; high volume and recurrence make Isaiah 60 a primary source for the section.

echoes.text: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.
echoes.note: 'Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead' (v.14) takes up 'Your dead shall live... awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust,' the resurrection-awakening oracle. High coherence with the rouse-from-death imagery; a leading source for the cited hymn.

echoes.text: For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you.
echoes.note: 'Darkness shall cover the earth... but the LORD will arise upon you' continues the darkness-over-against-light contrast that structures 5:8-11. Medium volume; reinforces the Isaian source of the whole light/darkness paraenesis.

echoes.text: Woe to those who deeply hide their counsel from Yahweh, and whose works are in the dark, and who say, “Who sees us?” and “Who knows us?”
echoes.note: 'Woe to those who hide deep their counsel from the LORD, whose deeds are in the dark' lies behind 'the unfruitful works of darkness... done in secret.' Coherence is strong (hidden/secret deeds exposed by light); medium confidence given thematic rather than lexical tie.

echoes.text: “These are of those who rebel against the light. They don’t know its ways, nor stay in its paths. The murderer rises with the light. He kills the poor and needy. In the night he is like a thief. The eye also of the adulterer waits for the twilight, saying, ‘No eye shall see me.’ He disguises his face. In the dark they dig through houses. They shut themselves up in the daytime. They don’t know the light. For the morning is to all of them like thick […]
echoes.note: Job's 'rebels against the light' who work murder and adultery in darkness, for whom morning is deep darkness, supplies the wisdom topos of secret works of darkness exposed. Medium volume; coherent with Ephesians' light-reveals-shameful-deeds logic.

echoes.text: Awake, awake, stand up, Jerusalem, that have drunk at the hand of Yahweh the cup of his wrath; you have drunken the bowl of the cup of staggering, and drained it.
echoes.note: 'Rouse yourself, rouse yourself, stand up, O Jerusalem' contributes the awakening-summons cadence behind 'Awake, you who sleep.' Medium volume; one of the clustered Isaian wake-up calls underlying the v.14 hymn.

echoes.text: Awake, awake, put on your strength, Zion; put on your beautiful garments, Jerusalem, the holy city: for henceforth there shall no more come into you the uncircumcised and the unclean.
echoes.note: 'Awake, awake, put on your strength, O Zion' is the paired imperatival summons (egeirou) that, with 60:1, shapes the hymnic 'Awake... and Christ will shine on you.' Coherence with the awakening-then-glory sequence is strong.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: 'Many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake' offers an apocalyptic resurrection idiom for the sleeper rising from the dead in v.14. Low volume relative to the Isaian sources; flagged for the sleep-then-awake-from-death recurrence.

echoes.text: But to you who fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings. You will go out, and leap like calves of the stall.
echoes.note: 'The sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings' faintly informs 'Christ will shine on you' (epiphausei). Low volume and contested; included for the rising-light-upon-the-awakened motif.

echoes.text: But the path of the righteous is like the dawning light, that shines more and more until the perfect day.
echoes.note: 'The path of the righteous is like the light of dawn, shining brighter' supports the 'walk as children of light' / 'fruit of light in goodness and righteousness' wisdom imagery. Low confidence; thematic coherence with the righteous-walk-in-light topos.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: you shall not bow yourself down to them, nor serve them, for I, Yahweh your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, on the third and on the fourth generation of those who hate me,
echoes.note: The disciples' question 'who sinned, this man or his parents' presupposes the Decalogue principle of God visiting the iniquity of fathers upon children. The transgenerational logic is precisely what is at issue; Volume is moderate and Coherence high, since Johannine sin-theology engages the retribution framework only to overturn it.

echoes.text: The soul who sins, he shall die: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be on him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be on him.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's countervailing principle that 'the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father' frames the very debate the disciples raise. Jesus' answer ('neither did this man sin, nor his parents') aligns with Ezekiel's repudiation of inherited guilt, making this a coherent and available Second-Temple intertext.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to him, “Who made man’s mouth? Or who makes one mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Isn’t it I, Yahweh?
echoes.note: YHWH to Moses: 'Who makes a man dumb or deaf, or seeing or blind? Is it not I, the LORD?' This grounds blindness in God's sovereign purpose, exactly Jesus' reframing ('that the works of God might be revealed'). Coherence is high since the giver of sight here becomes incarnate as the light-bringer.

echoes.text: “Remember, now, whoever perished, being innocent? Or where were the upright cut off?
echoes.note: The friends' assumption that suffering proves prior sin (Eliphaz: 'who ever perished, being innocent?') is the wisdom-debate background to the disciples' question. Job as a whole resists the suffering-equals-sin calculus; the echo is thematic and diffuse rather than verbal.

echoes.text: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you. For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you. Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.
echoes.note: 'I am the light of the world' resonates with Zion's eschatological illumination where YHWH's light shines on a darkened earth. The light-of-the-nations motif is available and coherent with John's worldwide scope, though no verbal citation links them.

echoes.text: Yahweh is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear? Yahweh is the strength of my life. Of whom shall I be afraid?
echoes.note: 'The LORD is my light and my salvation' supplies a scriptural backdrop for Jesus' self-identification as light, especially apposite as a blind man is about to receive sight/salvation. The echo is conceptual; Volume is low and many candidates compete.

echoes.text: “Because this people have refused the waters of Shiloah that go softly, and rejoice in Rezin and Remaliah’s son;
echoes.note: John glosses Siloam as 'Sent,' and the pool's name derives from the gently-flowing 'waters of Shiloah' that Judah despised in Isaiah 8:6. The deliberate etymological note signals figural intent: the rejected waters become the means of sight, and 'Sent' identifies Jesus as the one sent by the Father. High Volume via the explicit gloss.

echoes.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped.
echoes.note: 'Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened' is the eschatological sign of God's coming; the actual opening of a blind man's eyes enacts it. The healing is a programmatic fulfillment-sign, and John repeatedly frames Jesus' works as the dawning of the promised age. High Coherence and Recurrence across Isaiah's sight oracles.

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: Jesus forms mud from spittle and the ground and applies it to make eyes whole, evoking the Creator forming the man from the dust of the ground. The clay-and-creation figure casts the healing as a new-creation act by the agent of Genesis 1's 'let there be light'; Coherence with the light-of-the-world saying is strong.

echoes.text: Elisha sent a messenger to him, saying, “Go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and your flesh shall come again to you, and you shall be clean.”
echoes.note: 'Go, wash' in a specific body of water and be made whole closely patterns Elisha's command to Naaman to wash in the Jordan and be cleansed. The prophetic-healing-by-washing type, with obedience producing restoration, is coherent and the man's later confession that Jesus is 'a prophet' reinforces the Elijah/Elisha matrix.

echoes.text: By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”
echoes.note: The 'ground/dust' material of the healing recalls the adamic dust to which humanity belongs. The reversal — dust here restores rather than condemns — supports a new-creation reading, though the link rides on the same Genesis 2-3 imagery as the stronger 2:7 echo.

echoes.text: The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until he comes to whom it belongs. To him will the obedience of the peoples be.
echoes.note: The Hebrew 'Shiloh' ('until Shiloh comes') was read messianically in Second-Temple tradition and shares the consonantal root behind Siloam/'Sent.' John's 'Sent One' Christology may exploit this resonance, but the linguistic bridge is contested and the gloss more naturally targets Isaiah's Shiloah.

echoes.text: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness.
echoes.note: 'In that day...the eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity' supplies the eschatological frame as neighbors marvel that the beggar now sees. The pericope is largely narrative dialogue, so the echo is ambient rather than pointed, carried over from the healing itself.

echoes.text: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.
echoes.note: The conflict turns on Jesus 'making mud' and healing on the Sabbath, engaging the Decalogue's Sabbath command and its later halakhic elaborations (kneading clay was forbidden work). The Sabbath statute is the legal axis of the Pharisees' charge that Jesus is 'not from God.'

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.
echoes.note: The healed man's verdict 'He is a prophet' invokes the Mosaic promise of a prophet like Moses whom Israel must heed. John develops the prophet-like-Moses Christology, and the sign-working healer fits the criterion of the true prophet; Coherence with John's wider Moses typology is strong.

echoes.text: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established.
echoes.note: The interrogation of the parents to corroborate the son's testimony reflects the Torah's two-or-three-witnesses requirement that governs Johannine 'witness' motifs. The link is structural/legal rather than verbal, and the courtroom framing is broadly Deuteronomic.

echoes.text: Joshua said to Achan, “My son, please give glory to Yahweh, the God of Israel, and make confession to him. Tell me now what you have done! Don’t hide it from me!”
echoes.note: 'Give glory to God' is a near-verbatim adjuration formula: Joshua so charges Achan to confess before God in a judicial setting. The Pharisees use the identical oath-formula to pressure the man to recant, marking his testimony as sworn courtroom speech. High Volume via the fixed idiom.

echoes.text: If I cherished sin in my heart, the Lord wouldn’t have listened.
echoes.note: 'If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me' is closely paraphrased by 'God does not listen to sinners, but to the worshiper who does his will.' The man invokes a wisdom-psalm axiom about answered prayer to argue Jesus is from God. High Coherence and near-propositional match.

echoes.text: Yahweh is far from the wicked, but he hears the prayer of the righteous.
echoes.note: 'The LORD is far from the wicked, but he hears the prayer of the righteous' is the proverbial doublet behind 9:31's 'God does not listen to sinners but to the worshiper who does his will.' Recurrence with Psalm 66:18 strengthens both as the wisdom substrate of the man's argument.

echoes.text: Since then, there has not arisen a prophet in Israel like Moses, whom Yahweh knew face to face,
echoes.note: 'We are disciples of Moses... God has spoken to Moses' echoes the Torah's claim that no prophet arose like Moses, whom YHWH knew face to face. The Pharisees stake authority on Mosaic revelation, the very framework John uses to argue Jesus surpasses Moses. Coherence high within the chapter's Moses polemic.

echoes.text: With him, I will speak mouth to mouth, even plainly, and not in riddles; and he shall see Yahweh’s form. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant, against Moses?”
echoes.note: 'With him I speak mouth to mouth' grounds the unique standing of Moses claimed by 'God has spoken to Moses.' The Pharisees' 'we know God has spoken to Moses, but we don't know where this man is from' trades on this Mosaic-speech privilege. Available and coherent with the disciples-of-Moses boast.

echoes.text: When you spread out your hands, I will hide my eyes from you. Yes, when you make many prayers, I will not hear. Your hands are full of blood.
echoes.note: 'When you spread out your hands I will hide my eyes... I will not hear' supplies the prophetic version of God refusing to hear sinners. It reinforces 9:31 alongside the psalm and proverb, broadening the 'God hears the righteous' axiom across Torah-Prophets-Writings.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s eyes are toward the righteous. His ears listen to their cry.
echoes.note: 'The eyes of the LORD are toward the righteous, and his ears toward their cry' is a further wisdom witness to the principle that God hears the God-fearing but not the wicked. It coheres with 9:31 and adds Recurrence, though the man's wording is closest to Psalm 66:18 and Proverbs 15:29.

echoes.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped.
echoes.note: 'Since the world began it was never heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind' frames the sign as unprecedented — only God can do the eschatological eye-opening of Isaiah 35:5. The man's argument turns the prophetic sign-act into proof of divine origin. Coherence with the chapter's controlling Isaianic motif.

echoes.text: Yahweh opens the eyes of the blind. Yahweh raises up those who are bowed down. Yahweh loves the righteous.
echoes.note: 'The LORD opens the eyes of the blind' names eye-opening as a distinctly divine work, undergirding 'if this man were not from God he could do nothing.' The man reasons exactly along the psalm's lines, attributing a God-only act to Jesus. Strong Coherence with John's high Christology.

echoes.text: Therefore you shall make images of your tumors, and images of your mice that mar the land; and you shall give glory to the God of Israel: perhaps he will lighten his hand from off you, and from off your gods, and from off your land.
echoes.note: 'Give glory to the God of Israel' as a confessional demand recurs in the Philistine episode, reinforcing the formula behind 9:24. It is a secondary witness to the same idiom rather than an independent source; Joshua 7:19 is the closer judicial parallel.

echoes.text: He will not accept any person against a poor man; And he will listen to the prayer of him that is wronged. He will in no wise despise the supplication of the fatherless; Nor the widow, when she pours out her tale. Do not the tears of the widow run down her cheek? And is not her cry against him that has caused them to fall? He that serves God according to his good pleasure shall be accepted, And his supplication shall reach to the clouds.
echoes.note: Ben Sira affirms that God hears the prayer of the humble and the one who serves him with his whole heart, a deuterocanonical articulation of the doctrine in 9:31. Available within Second-Temple piety and coherent, though the canonical psalm/proverb are the nearer sources.

echoes.text: He said, “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand; and you see indeed, but don’t perceive.’ Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”
echoes.note: 'I came for judgment, that those who don't see may see, and those who see may become blind' inverts and fulfills Isaiah's commission to blind the seeing and deafen the hearing. John elsewhere cites Isaiah 6:10 explicitly (12:40), making this the controlling intertext for the chapter's sight/blindness-as-judgment theme. High Recurrence and Coherence.

echoes.text: “Hear, you deaf, and look, you blind, that you may see. Who is blind, but my servant? Or who is as deaf as my messenger whom I send? Who is as blind as he who is at peace, and as blind as Yahweh’s servant? You see many things, but don’t observe. His ears are open, but he doesn’t listen.
echoes.note: 'Who is blind but my servant... seeing many things, but you do not observe' supplies the prophetic paradox of those who possess sight yet remain blind, mirroring the Pharisees who 'see' yet have sin remaining. Coherent with the judicial blinding motif and available within the Isaianic servant oracles.

echoes.text: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness.
echoes.note: 'In that day the deaf shall hear... and the eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity and darkness' frames the chapter's resolution: a blind man comes to physical and spiritual sight while the seeing are darkened. The double movement realizes Isaiah's reversal-of-perception oracle and coheres with the light/darkness frame.

echoes.text: Bring out the blind people who have eyes, and the deaf who have ears.
echoes.note: 'Bring forth the people who are blind, yet have eyes, and the deaf who have ears' reinforces the sighted-yet-blind paradox applied to the Pharisees. Secondary to Isaiah 6 and 42; adds Recurrence to the Isaianic blindness cluster but contributes little independently.

echoes.text: Pause and wonder! Blind yourselves and be blind! They are drunken, but not with wine; they stagger, but not with strong drink. For Yahweh has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep, and has closed your eyes, the prophets; and he has covered your heads, the seers.
echoes.note: Isaiah's stupefied, blinded leaders ('they are blind... the LORD has poured on you a spirit of deep sleep, and has closed your eyes') parallel the self-confident Pharisees judged blind. The judicial-blinding theme coheres, though the verbal contact is faint amid the stronger Isaiah 6 link.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: 'Do you believe in the Son of Man?' (a strong textual variant for 'Son of God') invokes the Danielic Son of Man before whom worship is rendered, fitting the man's response of belief and worship in 9:38. The link depends on the variant reading, so confidence is low though the title is Danielic.

registers.label: Spare
lines: The Lord does not see as we see; the Lord looks on the heart.
Open our eyes; we want to see.
Once we were blind, and we washed, and now we see.
The Lord is our light; whom shall we fear?
Wake, O sleeper, and rise; let Christ shine on you.
Once we were darkness; now we are light in the Lord.
The Shepherd leads us home; come, let us worship.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Imagine a lifetime of darkness, only voices and heat and the feel of the road, and then mud, and water, and light pouring in.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
This is what God does: passes over the tall and the likely, takes the youngest in from the sheep, and pours the oil on his head.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
For the Lord looks past the face we show the world and reads the heart we hide, and calls us anyway.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
Wake, sleeper; rise from where you have lain; the light of Christ is already on your face.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
The Shepherd walks us through the valley to a table spread in the open. Come, let us worship.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross. Give us light. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: The Lord looks not on the face but on the heart.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
We washed in the pool, and the light came flooding in.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
Wake, O sleeper; Christ will shine on you.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
The Shepherd leads us home. Come, let us worship.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross. Amen.
